name: Bonefish
takeNotes: They eat down, off the bottom, and you rarely see the fly go in — you see the fish tip, or the line comes tight. Strip set. A trout set pulls the fly out of the zone and ends the shot.
fightNotes: First run is the whole fight. Clear the line, get them on the reel, keep the rod low to the side. Backing knots and a clean deck matter more than drag setting.
notes: Resident year-round in all three regions. Spookiness is the binding constraint: line slap, a fly landing on their head, or a shadow ends a shot before fly choice matters.
huntNotes: They hunt nose-down, rooting the bottom — tailing when it is shallow enough, mudding when it is not. A cruising fish covers ground fast and a feeding fish barely moves, and the two want completely different leads.
refusal: A follow that turns off means the fly was too big, too heavy, or moved too much. Go one size down and one weight class lighter before you change pattern.

name: Permit
takeNotes: The eat is slow and deliberate — the fish tips down on the crab. Do not strip once it commits; let it eat, then come tight.
fightNotes: Dogged and long. They use their body against the current.
notes: The realistic upgrade target on an early-spring Belize week, ahead of tarpon.
huntNotes: They swim down a crab deliberately and will track it for yards before committing. The decision happens slowly, which is exactly why it is easy to ruin.
refusal: A follow with no eat almost always means the fly swam. Let it die on the bottom and do nothing at all.

name: Tarpon
takeNotes: Keep stripping through the eat and strip-strike hard, more than once. A bony mouth throws a hook that was never driven.
fightNotes: Bow to every jump or the tippet pays for it.
notes: Two different fisheries wearing one name. Resident juveniles hold in back lagoons and river mouths year-round and fish on a 9-10 weight. Migratory adults arrive late April through August, peaking May into early July, run 60 to well over 100 lb, and need an 11-12 weight with a bite tippet. Conflating them is the most common planning mistake for this species.
huntNotes: They eat from below and ahead, rolling up onto something moving across them. A fly travelling toward a tarpon shuts it down; a fly leaving gets chased.
refusal: If they flare or sink out, the fly crossed their nose. Lead further, get it deeper, and swim it away from them.

name: False albacore
takeNotes: Lead the blitz, never cast into it. Fast, long strips — a fly that stops is a fly they refuse.
fightNotes: Straight down and fast. Loose line on the deck is how you lose them.
notes: Fall run off the NC coast, bait-driven rather than tide-driven. They show as water falls into the high 60s; the sweet spot is 58-64 degrees and it stays worth fishing into the low 50s. Best in October and November, peaking around the first week of November and running into December.
huntNotes: They run bait down at speed and slash through a ball of it. They are hunting the one that broke away, not the school.
refusal: A refusal means the fly is too big or it stopped. Go smaller and never stop stripping.

name: Redfish
takeNotes: They see poorly straight ahead. Put it close and move it a little.
fightNotes: Bulldogging, short runs, structure is the risk.
notes: Year-round backstop on the NC coast; best on a flooding marsh tide.
huntNotes: They root and tail in shallow water and see poorly straight ahead. The shot is close and the fly has to be found rather than chased.
refusal: If it ignores the fly it probably never saw it. Recast closer and move it a little, not more.

name: Cutthroat trout
takeNotes: Slow, confident rise on top — the classic mistake is setting before the fish has turned down.
fightNotes: Less frantic than a rainbow; they use current rather than speed.
notes: Forgiving compared with rainbows in the same water, which makes them the better target when the presentation is not perfect.
huntNotes: They hold in soft water beside fast water and let the current bring food to them. Finding the seam matters more than the fly.
refusal: A refusal on top usually means drag. Fix the drift before you change the fly.

name: Rainbow trout
takeNotes: Faster and more decisive than a cutthroat; a quick, short set.
fightNotes: Runs and jumps. Give line early.
huntNotes: They take stations in faster water than cutthroat will and move further for a fly, which makes them easier to find and quicker to spook.
refusal: Refusals usually mean size. Drop one hook size before you change pattern.

name: Brown trout
takeNotes: Streamer eats are often a follow and a refusal at the bank — keep the fly moving all the way in.
fightNotes: Heavy and low; they head for wood.
notes: Low light and off-color water are the conditions worth planning around.
huntNotes: They ambush. Big ones hunt on the edges of light — dusk, dawn, off-colour water — and follow a streamer a long way before committing or turning off.
refusal: A follow to the bank that turns away is a pause problem, not a fly problem. Let it hang before you lift.
